simple_description: A neurodevelopmental condition characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention (trouble focusing), hyperactivity (excessive restlessness), and impulsivity that interferes with daily functioning.
medical_description: A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that has a direct negative impact on academic, occupational, or social functioning. Symptoms emerge prior to age 12, persist for >= 6 months, and manifest across two or more settings (e.g. home and school/work).
affected_system: Prefrontal cortex executive control networks, basal ganglia, and frontostriatal dopamine and norepinephrine signaling.
symptoms: Inattention: making careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks, struggling to follow multi-step instructions, chronic disorganization
Forgetfulness in daily activities (losing keys, phone, forgetting appointments)
Hyperactivity: fidgeting with hands or feet, squirming in seat, feeling inwardly restless (in adults), talking excessively
Impulsivity: blurting out answers before questions are finished, difficulty waiting turns, interrupting conversations
Executive dysfunction: severe chronic procrastination and difficulty estimating time ('time blindness')
early_warning_signs: Consistently struggling with sustained attention and impulse control in classroom and home compared to same-age peers
possible_causes: High heritability (~75-80%; involving dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and receptor DRD4 genes)
Delayed maturation of prefrontal cortical thickness
risk_factors: Family history of ADHD, maternal smoking or alcohol during pregnancy, very low birth weight
clinical_evaluation: Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Rating Scale / Conners Scale (completed by parents and teachers), Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1).
diagnostic_tests: Comprehensive developmental and psychological clinical assessment
treatment_overview: Multimodal therapy combining behavioral interventions and pharmacotherapy. Psychostimulants (Methylphenidate, Amphetamines) are the most effective first-line medical treatment with response rates > 70-80%. Non-stimulants (Atomoxetine, Guanfacine, Clonidine) are effective alternatives.
medication_classes: First-line Stimulants: Methylphenidate (Ritalin / Concerta extended-release), Lisdexamfetamine / Mixed Amphetamine Salts
Non-stimulants: Atomoxetine (selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), Guanfacine ER (alpha-2A adrenergic agonist)
precautions: Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, and growth/weight regularly while on stimulant medications
prevention: Structured organizational routines, clear visual timers, broken-down checklists
complications: Academic underachievement, occupational instability, increased risk of accidental injuries, comorbid anxiety/depression
emergency_signs: Severe acute emotional dysregulation or impulsive dangerous behaviors
doctor_specialty: Child and Adolescent Psychiatrist / Developmental Pediatrician / Adult ADHD Specialist

faqs.question: Can adults have ADHD?
faqs.answer: Yes. While physical hyperactivity often decreases with age, inattention, disorganization, chronic procrastination, and restlessness frequently continue into adulthood.

hi.name: एडीएचडी / ध्यान की कमी और अतिसक्रियता (ADHD)
hi.summary: एक जगह ध्यान केंद्रित न कर पाना, अत्यधिक चंचलता (हाथ-पैर हिलाना) और बिना सोचे-समझे उतावलेपन में काम करना।
hi.advice: यह आलस नहीं बल्कि मस्तिष्क के डोपामाइन पाथवे का विकार है। बिहेवियर थेरेपी और डॉक्टर द्वारा दी जाने वाली दवाओं से सुधार होता है।

hinglish.name: ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder)
hinglish.summary: Padhai ya kaam me dhyan na lagna, baar-baar cheezein bhoolna, restless hona aur time management me fail hona.
hinglish.advice: Specialist psychiatrist se consult karein. Methylphenidate ya Atomoxetine aur behavioral coaching bohot helpful hai.
